pages:
Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

Digital Operations & AI Automation

I’d like to join your team in a paid role looking after the website, customer follow-up, and simple AI tools that save time.

I’m new to the electrical business, and I won’t pretend otherwise. I’d start by learning how you already work, then help wherever you tell me it’s useful. You’d approve anything a customer sees.

Where I’d start

Two small website fixes, quick to check and easy to undo, plus one simple follow-up habit in the software you already use.

  • Point emergencies to the phone. The contact form lets people choose “Emergency Service.” A short line beside it could say: “For an emergency, please call (727) 761-7767 now.”
  • Ask where the job is. A city or ZIP box on the contact form, so no one has to call back just to check the area.
  • Keep track of every request. For each customer message: who has it, what happens next, and by when.

Please read these as questions, not corrections. You know your customers far better than I do.

We’d agree before starting: hours and pay, what I can access, who approves the work, and when we’d look at the results together.

Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

What I’ve already built

An example dashboard for incoming messages

Calls, emails, texts, and website messages land in one place, and emergencies rise to the top. AI helpers sort the rest into electrical, office, and website lanes, each with a person in charge. They pull out the key details and draft a reply. A person approves every reply and handles every emergency.

Try it: adamjskoog.github.io/sspros-proposal/dashboard.html. Every message is made up, and nothing is sent.

How the AI did in testing

I tested the website-message sorting on 40 made-up messages I wrote. 39 of 40 passed the automatic checks, and all 6 emergencies went to a person. It still made mistakes: one answer made up details about the website form.

A test I wrote myself doesn’t prove it works on real messages. Your team would check it on real work before relying on it.

Where AI could help next

  • Turning the estimator’s notes into a clean written proposal. A person sets every price.
  • Service reminders for generator and EV charger customers.
  • Turning a voice memo from the job site into a tidy job note.

Also built: a sample page for commercial work, 38 website ideas, and an office kit with a workbook and four message drafts.

Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

A measured start

The first 90 days

Weeks 1–2: listen

Learn how a customer request moves through your office and which software you already use. Bring back a short list of suggestions for you to choose from.

By day 30: first results

One website fix you approved, live and checked. One simple follow-up habit in the system you already use, so no customer is forgotten.

By day 60: one AI task

Try the AI idea you picked on real work, with a person checking everything it produces. Keep track of the time it takes, including the checking.

Day 90: decide together

Keep it, change it, or stop it, based on what actually happened. Agree the ongoing role, hours, and pay.

What we’d watch: how quickly customers hear back, whether requests arrive complete, that nothing is forgotten, and the time spent, including checking the AI’s work.

AI tool budget

Between $120 and $400 a month, depending on the plans you choose, and never more than $400 including tax. Hours and pay are separate. Starter: one tool on its $100 plan and the other on its $20 plan ($120). Middle: both on $100 plans ($200). Full: both on $200 plans ($400). A company plan, such as Claude Team or ChatGPT Business, is also an option. No automatic top-ups; any change needs written approval.

Let’s choose the first piece of work to own.

A 30-minute conversation to understand your priorities and agree whether this starting role makes sense. Text or call Adam: 805-624-0580.

website-review.html.title: SSPros website research appendix
pages:
Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

Website observations and priorities

I read your public website carefully and wrote down what I noticed. I’d also like to ask for a paid role helping with the website and the office.

A note before you read: I’m new to the electrical business. I wrote this from the public website only. I don’t know your customers, your history, or why things are set up the way they are. Please read everything here as questions and ideas, not as instructions.

Start with a small, checked change

Confirm company facts first, then improve the inquiry handoff. Consider service-page expansion when it supports the company’s priorities. The current role and assignment are described in the proposal and short summary.

Three public-page observations

  • The homepage lists 50+ completed projects; About lists 500+. Confirm what each total means before changing it.
  • The contact form does not show a dedicated project-city or ZIP field. Confirm whether adding one helps more than it burdens completion.
  • Homepage service links lead to a shared services page. Consider a focused destination for one priority service.

Public-page review dated November 1, 2026; core observations checked during the November 3 review. These observations do not establish lost sales.

Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

Confirm facts and choose the work

Other items from the public review

  • The headline “Licensed. Insured. Done Right.” emphasizes trust; test whether naming the work more directly improves understanding.
  • Coverage descriptions should be checked for consistent meaning. Public copy includes statewide wording; confirm any regional or service-specific limits.
  • The earlier review found Privacy and Terms links returning to the homepage. Recheck their destinations before choosing the correction.
  • Small wording errors include “Industry Experiance” and “across throughout Florida.”

Use primary facts

The company should confirm service scope, coverage, counts, credentials, response commitments, and permissions for photos. An external directory is a lead to check, not a reason to overwrite company facts.

Sources and completion

Public sources: sspro.us, sspro.us/about, sspro.us/services, and sspro.us/contact. Keep an approved source, owner, and review date with any factual change.

Finished means the approved version is delivered and checked, with affected links and request handoffs working. An agreed preview is a valid deliverable when publication access is outside the assignment.

The following 38 ideas are a backlog. Select a small scope based on the company’s priorities and existing systems.

Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

The basic customer journey

First: confirm facts and the inquiry handoff.

  1. Agree on one short description of what you do, and use it everywhere.
  2. Keep one sheet of approved facts: project counts, license, phone, and hours.
  3. Write down exactly which areas you serve.
  4. Put what you do in the homepage headline.
  5. Keep the menu short, with everyday words.
  6. Give business, low-voltage, and home customers their own starting point.
  7. Make each service link open that service.
  8. Add a city or ZIP box to the contact form.
  9. Make it easy to tap and call from a phone.
  10. Send an agreed test message through the form to make sure it arrives.

Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

Help customers decide

Next: select content and pages that support priority services.

  1. Keep the emergency number clearly separate from the estimate form.
  2. Fix the Privacy and Terms links after confirming their intended destinations.
  3. Give each type of work a short overview page.
  4. Write pages for the services you most want to be known for.
  5. Explain how an estimate starts and what happens next.
  6. Use real photos of your work and team, with permission.
  7. Show finished projects, grouped by type of work.
  8. Write short project stories: the need, the work, and the result.
  9. Show where any rating or review comes from.
  10. Introduce the people behind the company.

Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

Keep information consistent

Choose confirmed corrections first; expand content when there is an owner.

  1. Word the license consistently on every page, using approved facts.
  2. Add a page listing the areas you serve.
  3. Answer the questions customers ask most.
  4. Proofread every page.
  5. Keep fonts, colors, and buttons consistent.
  6. Check pages on phones and tablets.
  7. Check keyboard access, labels, readability, and contrast.
  8. Give each page a clear title describing its subject.
  9. Confirm the correct public business address, hours, and phone.
  10. Match approved details across listings on other websites.

Prepared for System Solutions Pros · January 2027

Test and maintain the work

Keep checks and upkeep alongside each change.

  1. Make photos load efficiently.
  2. Keep old links pointing to a useful destination.
  3. Measure page loading on a phone.
  4. Test the menu, buttons, and form before changes go live.
  5. If useful and approved, count form messages and phone taps.
  6. Note which requests fit the work the company wants.
  7. Compare later results with the starting measurement.
  8. Assign responsibility for keeping each part of the website current.

The current office kit

Three routines cover customer follow-up, website updates, and the weekly handoff. The kit includes a workbook with blank tabs and fictional examples, CSV alternatives, instructions, and four editable message drafts. It does not send reminders or connect to company systems.

Use the company’s existing system where it already handles this work. Keep a private working copy and use source links rather than duplicating unnecessary customer details.
